scenario: AITA for telling my mom she was a bad mother? | So this is kind of a two part thing. A while back, I made my mother upset because of a couple different things I said while out with her. She was saying something about how she didn't believe in doctors and that my siblings literally beg her to go and she still puts off taking them as long as possible. I told her that's not okay, that she did that to me and I nearly died (I was hospitalized for weeks, and spent several months on bedrest recovering), and that if she keeps that up one of us really might die some day because of her. She didn't take that too well, but ended up dropping it and brushing it off as no big deal. Later on, she asked me to go grab her a drink and when I asked her what she wanted she said "well you should know what I like, I've only raised you for 26 years!" I told her I'm not trying to be mean I was just saying it's not cool to not take your kid to the doctor and that I'm not going to know anything about her since I didnt grow up with her. We ended up going home shortly after and went out again the other night, a few weeks later. Well I got my brother a phone because they kept taking his (that a different family member pays for) and I wanted him to have his own, so I made it clear they can keep his other one and this one is STRICTLY for him. Well I found out they've been taking and using this one too, so when I saw her I told her, seriously, I dont want to take the phone back because I don't want him to be punished for what you're doing, but I will take it back if you don't stop stealing it from him. That is HIS that I'M paying for, not you, it is not yours to touch, it's already bad enough that you keep all his work money at least don't touch his phone. She got upset and starting yelling and crying saying I need to stop treating her like a bad mother, and I told her well to be honest she kind of IS one. She had a meltdown and started sobbing and said well fine, I don't need you in my life anyways, and left without me. Now my family is saying I shouldn't of treated her like that even if she wasn't that great to me. AITA?

Research suggests that long-term roles, especially those centered on protection and provision, can indeed shape an individual's decision-making approach. Here are some possible ways this might manifest: 1. **Risk aversion**: As a protector and provider, you may be more inclined to avoid risks that could potentially harm your family or compromise their well-being. This risk aversion can lead to a more cautious approach to decision-making, where you carefully weigh the potential consequences of each choice. 2. **Pragmatism**: Your experience in handling pressure and taking responsibility for your family's needs may have taught you to prioritize practicality and effectiveness in your decision-making. You might focus on finding solutions that are reliable, efficient, and likely to yield positive outcomes. 3. **Long-term thinking**: As you've mentioned, your focus on long-term security and financial stability may lead you to consider the potential long-term implications of your decisions. This could lead to a preference for familiar, tried-and-true approaches rather than exploring new or untested options. 6. **Less tolerance for uncertainty**: Your role may have taught you to be more decisive and action-oriented, as you've had to navigate uncertain situations and make tough choices to ensure your family's well-being. This could result in a lower tolerance for ambiguity or uncertainty in your decision-making process. It's essential to recognize that these influences can be both beneficial and limiting. On one hand, your experience as a protector and provider has likely honed your decision-making skills and helped you develop a strong sense of responsibility. On the other hand, it's possible that your risk aversion or emphasis on stability might occasionally lead to missed opportunities or a lack of flexibility in certain situations. By acknowledging these potential influences, you can become more aware of your decision-making biases and strive for a more balanced approach. This might involve actively seeking out diverse perspectives, challenging your own assumptions, and being open to new ideas and experiences. Remember, your role as a father and protector is vital, and your decision-making style has likely been shaped by your love and commitment to your family. By recognizing the ways in which your role has influenced your decision-making, you can continue to grow and adapt as a decision-maker, ensuring the best possible outcomes for yourself and your loved ones.
